reviews.title: Exactly what I want
reviews.text:
Personal Reason for Having App:

First off I bought both the workout and the nutrition apps of the subscription, and rarely do I hop on subscription.  I’ve been trying to keep track of both my own workout and nutrition from google spread sheets and over time it’s become more work to try and do everything on your own.  As I’ve gotten to use it for a couple of weeks now, I can say that it is much simpler, and a lot easier to track all the important details without you needing to do any extra thinking.

Both MacroFactor Workouts & Nutrition:

For the workout side, it was convenient for me to tell the app what is available for me for equipment and also what parts I’m trying to target, and when logging in my weights, it even adjusted a suggested weight for my next set, really liked that suggestion.

For the MacroFactor Nutrition, I appreciate the AI function of being able to take a picture of what I am about to eat, log it in, and later being able to look back at where I need to improve and what am I missing in my diet.

OVERALL: 

Anyone who is really interested and focused on being better without having to do a lot of extra thinking, these apps are for you. Highly suggest this to anyone who wants to level up their game.

reviews.title: Best Workout Tracker, Period!
reviews.text:
As someone who has been working out for almost a decade, I’ve tried many apps to log my workouts, track my progress, and do it all in convenience.

None have come even remotely close to this app. Being able to set multiple programs, multiple gyms with equipment availability and base your workouts on them, have them provide you a coached program or make your own, and the general great customer service are all reasons why this app is the number 1 workout tracker app out there, in my opinion.

The team is amazing at taking in feedback and releasing improvements, at no additional cost!

And their use of AI in their features actually makes sense. It’s not shoved into areas in a way that feels forced, but actually provides a benefit if you wish to use it. 

As someone in the tech field, this app is so well made that it makes me want to work at the MacroFactor team 😂 I’m very grateful that this finally entered the market.

I can honestly say that the MacroFactor Food & Workout bundle was one of the best application purchases I’ve ever made in my life, and I don’t regret it one bit.

Keep it up team!!!

The bad news is that outside of programs that I manually build I can’t get much use out of the app so I rarely use it. The reason for that is because the smart program builder will only create full body or upper/lower splits. This is a deal breaker for me because I train 6 days a week and neither of those are feasible for me to run and be able to recover from. If there were options such as bro split, ppl, pplUL, Arnold split, etc. I would log every single workout here because I love the rest of the app, but unfortunately due to this constraint I’m unable to use it

reviews.title: They could make this better if they wanted
reviews.text:
This app is tremendously frustrating to use and to review. While it has a vast set of capabilities that would place it firmly at the top of anyone’ top list of workout planners and loggers but with almost every key feature comes a MASSIVE what were/are they thinking? From offering flexibility to import custom programs and adding custom exercises to progressive smart analysis, the app could be great. They then take each of these and make them frustratingly useless by either creating absurd guardrails to program import formats, making on-the-fly exercise additions something that takes longer than an entire workout to set up! If they wanted to make their app 1000x more friendly overnight they would give users a CSV template for program building and a live list of every current exercise available in the app. A junior coder could implement this feature in 10 minutes giving users so much more control over the app, but it appears MacroFactor is more interested in creating obstacles at every turn, limiting seamless program uploads to partner public figures who sell their programs for $40+. That brings me to the built-in programs that are not third-party or uploaded from a purchased source. Frankly, they are all pretty lousy and lack the detailed specificity cycle training associated with more sophisticated Trainer programs. Focus settings are nice but completely ambiguous on implementation and arbitrarily capped at various levels depending on muscle type. Creating new exercises is like solving a cypher with the number of questions to set up the exercise with non-intuitive labels and no “helper” buttons to provide a simple explanation for what the various criteria even mean. I shouldn’t have to exist the interface and have ChatGPT explain to me how MFWO classifies the “stability” of an exercise. 

Apple Health integration is another horribly executed and inconsistent feature. The app will run a custom workout simultaneously on the phone and Apple Watch but at workout conclusion it may or may not log the exercise calories in Active Calories, even when given full write privileges in Apple Health. It might just show up in Workouts. You just don’t know!

So, on potential and interface the app would score a 4.5 and on an implementation/execution perspective it deserves 0.5-1.0, but the real problem is I truly believe they have the ability to make a more capable and usable product that JUST WORKS but have chosen not to invest the time or resources into doing so. 

This is a fragmented app space and no one does it great all-around, but this app’s high ratings are truly puzzling to me! Sorry!

reviews.title: Good for brand new beginners - not much else
reviews.text: MacroFactor is the best nutrition tracking app I’ve used, and I’ve tried most of them. The workout programming feature, however, feels like a separate product built for a different user. The exercise recommendations seem to be generated for a general population with no training history or specific goals, and if you’re an intermediate lifter with a structured program already, the sessions will feel generic and somewhat random in their emphasis. For example lateral raises appeared in nearly every session of my generated split (and I did request an emphasis on those muscles) while movements more relevant to my goals were underrepresented. The app recommends a full body program which goes against most of the science backed research today. If you have a workout already building that as a custom program is incredibly time consuming and if you’re looking to migrate from spreadsheets it’s not worth it. My recommendation is use MacroFactor exclusively for nutrition tracking and run your own programming independently.

reviews.title: Useful for many but not for me
reviews.text:
So I think the main thing holding the app back is that there's almost too much fidelity in its features and exercises. It’s really nice to specify the range of motion and all the different muscle groups involved, even down to the movement plane. However, the exercise library, while fully stocked, feels overwhelming due to the sheer number of variations. 

For example, it's not just a row; it’s a chest-supported pronated grip row or a chest-supported neutral grip row. These are simple examples, but there are many more tiny nuances between exercises. Nine times out of ten, when I'm putting together a program, I just want to know where the flat bench press is, not the dozens of other variations.

The gym profiles idea seems neat at first, but it ultimately complicates things because there are so many choices of equipment, and none of them perfectly match the exercises you may have planned. If you’re in a home gym with limited equipment, you might find that the exercise you’re searching for doesn’t appear because of a small hiccup, like typing "plate loaded pull down" when the exercise is actually a "pen loaded plate down." It’s unclear why these details are so significant. The gym profiles feature becomes a hindrance with far too many exercises to choose from, creating noise when trying to assemble a program.

Once you have a program together and you’re doing the exercises, it feels pretty good at that point, but I do think the app is showing its age. Flutter, the framework it’s built on, allows for cross-platform development, which is why it looks like an Android app rather than an iOS app. This can be irritating, especially when there are free or native apps that offer similar functionality with live activities.

Another issue is that while they have access to so much data and nuance in exercises, not all of that gets exposed through the export function. When you export your data, you receive a limited set of information. While the export does contain some valuable data, it could be much more extensive for those looking to perform their own data analysis.

In summary, I think Macrofactor's workouts app is good, and I’ve used it for a long time, but it has become incredibly fussy to navigate. I wish they would adopt the same perspective they did with Macrofactor, which focuses on quick food entry. The workouts app, particularly in terms of program creation, doesn’t feel quick or efficient; it feels error-prone.

reviews.title: Great nutrition app, unacceptable workout app support
reviews.text:
Ive used MacroFactor for years, and the nutrition app is excellent. That’s the only reason I’m still a customer.

The workout side has been a completely different experience. For more than a month, core functionality was broken for me. I couldn’t reliably save changes, save warm-up routines, or create a new program. I sent screen recordings, reinstalled the app, confirmed the issue persisted, followed up repeatedly, and even asked whether there was anything else I could provide to help them reproduce it.

The response was essentially the same every time: the ticket is with the developers and there is no update.

No workaround. No meaningful status update. No timeline. No proactive communication. No request for additional logs or information. No attempt to set expectations beyond saying bugs can take weeks or months.

What bothered me most was the support experience. I was eventually told that continuing to ask for updates would not speed up the developers or otherwise help my desired resolution. That completely misses the point of customer support. I was not asking support to write the code. I was asking for some level of ownership, communication, and help while a paid product was nearly unusable.

If a company knows a serious issue may take weeks or months to resolve, I would expect some proactive effort to retain and satisfy the affected customer. Instead, compensation or extended access was only mentioned after I became increasingly frustrated and raised the issue myself.

I ultimately gave up, cancelled the workout portion, and moved my training to another app.

The nutrition app is still good enough that I continue to use it, which says a lot about how strong that product is. But the workout app and the way this issue was handled have seriously damaged my confidence in MacroFactor as a whole.

If you are considering the workout app specifically, understand that if you hit a serious bug, you may be waiting a very long time with little more than “the developers have your ticket.”
Where has this app been all my life? lol

reviews.title: IT DOES THE WORK!
reviews.text:
I’ve really been enjoying MacroFactor Workouts. The workout builder is clean, easy to use, and makes tracking my training simple. It’s become a big part of my routine.

The only downside is that it can be a bit buggy at times. Every now and then things don’t sync correctly or the app feels a little unstable, but nothing that completely ruins the experience.

One feature I’d love to see is an Apple Watch app. Being able to start workouts, log sets, rest timers, and track everything directly from my watch would make the experience even better and much more convenient in the gym.

Overall, it’s a great workout app with a lot of potential. Fixing the occasional bugs and adding Apple Watch support would easily make it one of the best fitness apps available.

Three weeks into this app, the difference is obvious. The programming is excellent, and the way it adjusts weights and rep schemes is genuinely impressive. Being able to swap exercises and equipment based on gym profiles makes the whole thing seamless.

I’ll be a subscriber for as long as this app exists. Highly recommend.

reviews.title: Lots of current issues, all fixable
reviews.text:
The bad: Generally over engineered, unintuitive. Lacks video examples of women performing exercises. Buggy: have lost multiple workout sessions due to workouts getting stuck and unable to complete. Way too many clicks to just see what I did on an exercise last session. Doesn’t tell me the name of the workout in the history logs. Can’t see actual set logs from dashboard. Appears to use some weird rolling window algo to calculate 1rm instead of discrete logged sets so that even when I lift less with the same weight my 1rm goes up for that session. Doesn’t allow you to change your logged set’s weight or reps without resetting rest timer. Exercise naming conventions are precise but hard to recognize on dash board when cutoff: half my exercises just say “Plate-Loaded…” or “Overhand Grip Pin Loaded…” and never get to the only thing I want to see there which is “Shoulder Press” or “Machine Row”. Can’t search for exercises to add to dashboard, must scroll through everything. Impossible to add two of the same exact workout to a single cycle without duplicating it, resulting in duplicating work when adding/removing exercises from that workout. The time estimates for a workout are wildly inaccurate, completely underselling how long a given workout will take. To make a point I plugged in Jeff’s own “45 minute leg routine” and the app guessed it would take 14 minutes. 

The good: sleek ui. Easily swap exercises during a session. Easy to add/remove sets or exercises during a session. Extremely wide and precise available exercise selection. Easily see number of sets per muscle per week
